title: Book teaches complete trading plan from entry to exit with specific price levels
claim: Unlike most trading books, this book teaches specific action sequences including exact buy/sell prices rather than vague guidance like 'buy around here'

source.section: High Probability Trade Strategies for Any Market and Any Time Frame

support: Author argues brokers only accept specific price orders, and vague conditional statements are not tradeable
mechanism: Book structure: recognize opportunity → exact entry price → exact stop price → exit management
failure_modes: Specific prices may be optimization-biased after-the-fact

title: Momentum strategy requires dual timeframe analysis
claim: Effective momentum trading uses two timeframes: a longer-term timeframe to confirm direction, and a shorter-term timeframe to identify entries
support: Author defines dual-timeframe momentum strategy as foundational approach
mechanism: Longer timeframe establishes trend bias; shorter timeframe triggers entry signal when momentum aligns with bias
failure_modes: Timeframe mismatch can generate false signals

title: Momentum and price trends often diverge
claim: Momentum indicators and price trends frequently diverge; when price makes new high but momentum does not, it signals weakening trend momentum
support: Author presents divergence as reliable signal of trend weakness and reversal opportunity
mechanism: Divergence indicates momentum is not confirming price trend, suggesting trend exhaustion
assumptions: Momentum indicators are valid measure of trend strength
failure_modes: Divergence can persist through prolonged trends (oversold/overbought rebounds)

title: Indicator selection is critical for momentum strategy success
claim: The book identifies multiple momentum indicators (RSI, MACD, Stochastics, Rate of Change) with different calculation windows; selection depends on market and timeframe

source.section: Which Indicators to Use for Multiple Time Frame Momentum Strategies

support: Author dedicates section to indicator choice and optimal settings discussion
mechanism: Different indicators have different lag, sensitivity, and false-signal rates; matching to market regime and timeframe improves signal quality
assumptions: Indicator lag and calibration matter for practical trading
failure_modes: Over-fitting to historical optimal settings; different market regimes require re-optimization

title: Elliott Wave overlap guideline distinguishes trends from corrections
claim: In Elliott Wave analysis, the overlap guideline determines whether price action is a trend or correction: if price retraces into the prior wave-one price range, it is a correction, not a new trend

source.section: Trend or Correction: The Overlap Guideline

support: Author presents overlap as primary objective criterion for pattern classification
mechanism: Trends display no price overlap into prior waves; corrections extend into and past prior wave overlap
assumptions: Price action strictly follows Elliott Wave rules
failure_modes: Overlap guideline is subjective when wave boundaries are not clear; can be gamed by small price excursions

title: Fifth-wave momentum is key to identifying trend completion
claim: In Elliott Wave five-wave trends, the fifth wave is key to identifying when a trend is complete; fifth waves often show lower momentum than earlier waves when trend is ending
support: Author emphasizes fifth-wave momentum as signal of trend exhaustion
mechanism: If fifth wave lacks momentum (divergence with earlier waves), it signals weak trend close and reversal opportunity
assumptions: Momentum divergence is measurable and predictive
failure_modes: Fifth waves can have strong momentum in some markets; rule not universal

title: Fibonacci retracements identify support/resistance for entries and exits
claim: Fibonacci retracement levels (38.2%, 50%, 61.8%) identify internal retracements within trends; external retracements beyond 100% identify potential reversal zones
support: Author uses Fibonacci levels as framework for identifying price targets and reversal zones
mechanism: Fibonacci ratios represent natural support/resistance levels in market price action
failure_modes: Fibonacci levels are ex-post rationalization; not predictive without other confluence

title: Pattern price targets derived from prior move relationships
claim: Price targets for new moves can be derived by measuring prior completed moves and projecting them forward using mathematical relationships (1x, 1.618x, 2x the prior move)
support: Author provides worked examples of price target calculation from prior swing lengths
mechanism: Market structure creates geometric relationships between successive moves; targets can be calculated before move completes
assumptions: Prior move relationships predict future move magnitude
failure_modes: Projection relationships not consistent across markets or regimes

title: Time retracements and time targets narrow entry windows
claim: Time retracements and time targets identify likely completion dates for price moves; combining price targets with time targets creates a time/price target zone for trade exits
support: Author presents time analysis as complementary to price analysis for identifying optimal exit windows
mechanism: Markets exhibit cyclical time patterns; time targets derived from prior move durations identify likely pivot dates
assumptions: Market time cycles are predictable from prior cycle durations
failure_modes: Time targets are imprecise; rarely produce exact-date pivots; subject to calendar artifacts (weekends, holidays)

title: Time bands represent likely reversal windows
claim: Time bands (calculated from Fibonacci ratios of prior cycle durations) indicate periods of high probability for trend reversals; multiple time bands can reinforce signal strength
support: Author shows convergence of multiple time bands as high-confidence reversal signal
mechanism: Fibonacci time ratios create confluence zones where reversals are more likely
assumptions: Fibonacci time ratios are predictive of reversal probability
failure_modes: Time bands frequently do not align with actual reversals; highly subjective selection of reference cycles

title: Trailing-bar entry captures trend momentum with tight stop
claim: Trailing-bar entry places buy order one tick above prior bar high (on an up-move); stop-loss is placed one tick below prior bar low; this captures momentum while limiting downside risk

source.section: Entry Strategy 1: Trailing One-Bar Entry and Stop

support: Author presents this as primary entry tactic for momentum trades
mechanism: New high on tight range suggests momentum continuation; tight stop prevents large loss if breakout fails
assumptions: One-bar breakouts are valid momentum signals
failure_modes: Whipsaws on breakouts generate many false signals and stop-outs; high transaction cost drag

title: Swing entry allows for larger stop placement and better risk/reward
claim: Swing entry places orders at Fibonacci retracement or 50% retracement of prior swing; stop is placed beyond the prior swing low, allowing larger risk for better reward potential

source.section: Entry Strategy 2: Swing Entry and Stop

support: Author contrasts swing entry with trailing-bar entry: higher reward/risk ratio but slower fill
mechanism: Entering on retracement rather than breakout reduces false signals; larger stop accommodates volatility and avoids noisy fills
assumptions: Fibonacci retracements provide valid entry zones
failure_modes: Retracement entries may enter after trend reversal completes; stop-placement is subjective

title: Position size should be inversely proportional to stop distance
claim: Position size calculation: smaller positions when stop-loss is distant, larger positions when stop is tight; this maintains constant dollar risk per trade across different market conditions
support: Author presents fixed-dollar-risk formula: position_size = fixed_risk_amount / (entry_price - stop_price)
mechanism: Ensures portfolio drawdown is controlled regardless of market volatility or chart setup
failure_modes: Does not account for correlation-driven portfolio blowups; assumes iid trades

title: Multiple-unit trading divides position into profit-taking tranches
claim: Sell portion of position at first price target, hold remainder for larger profit; this locks in gains while maintaining upside exposure
support: Author recommends exiting partial positions at 50% of Fibonacci target, then another tranche at full target
mechanism: Reduces pressure to exit whole position too early; captures some wins while allowing winners to run
assumptions: Partial exits are emotionally and operationally feasible
failure_modes: Partial exits create transaction costs; may lock in premature profits before large moves

title: Risk/reward ratio should exceed 1:2 before entry
claim: Do not enter a trade unless potential profit is at least 2x the stop-loss distance (i.e., 1:2 risk/reward minimum); this ensures winners exceed losers in magnitude
support: Author establishes 1:2 as minimum acceptable risk/reward; preferred setups offer 1:3 or 1:5
mechanism: Assuming 50% win rate, 1:2 ratio produces positive expectancy (0.5 * 2 - 0.5 * 1 = +0.5)
assumptions: Win rate is approximately 50% or higher
failure_modes: Win rate is often lower than 50% in real trading; ratio does not account for slippage/fees

title: Stop-loss should be adjusted upward as trade profits increase
claim: After trade reaches 50% of profit target, move stop to breakeven; after reaching another 50% of remaining profit, move stop to prior support; this locks in gains while preserving upside
support: Author provides stepped stop-adjustment rules for different profit levels
mechanism: Progressive trailing stop prevents large losses on trades that initially work but then reverse
assumptions: Trailing stops do not interfere with trade execution or create slippage
failure_modes: Trailing stops can be whipsawed out by noise; may exit winners prematurely

title: Trade only high-probability setups with confluence of multiple signals
claim: Do not trade every signal; wait for confluence of momentum, pattern, price, and time signals all aligned (high-probability setup); skip low-probability partial setups

source.section: Trade Only the High Probability, Optimum Setups

support: Author emphasizes selectivity: fewer trades with higher probability beats frequent trading of marginal setups
mechanism: Confluence of multiple independent signals reduces false-signal rate; improves win rate and average trade quality
assumptions: Multiple signal types are truly independent indicators
failure_modes: Confluence is subjective; overly selective approach may miss real moves

title: Traders should maintain detailed trade records and analyze outcomes
claim: Successful traders keep detailed records of every trade (entry, exit, stop, reason, outcome); regular analysis of these records identifies patterns in wins vs. losses
support: Author recommends daily review of trade records to identify recurring mistakes and strengths
mechanism: Data-driven feedback loop enables trader improvement and edge identification
assumptions: Trading outcomes are learnable from record analysis
failure_modes: Small sample sizes lead to spurious pattern recognition; confirmation bias in self-analysis

title: Trading success depends on plan adherence, not market prediction
claim: Successful traders follow a consistent plan regardless of market outlook; they do not try to predict market direction, but instead execute pre-defined rules when conditions are met
support: Author contrasts plan-followers (winners) with discretionary market-timers (losers)
mechanism: Plan adherence removes emotion; reduces over-trading and improves compliance to risk rules
assumptions: Plans are well-designed; traders can actually follow them
failure_modes: Plans may be sub-optimal; discipline is difficult under stress

title: Trade for points (targets), not ticks or price movement
claim: Successful traders trade toward a target price (a point in the market), not toward making the next tick move; this requires patience and discipline to wait for high-probability setups

source.section: Trade for Points, Not for Ticks

support: Author argues tick-counting is emotional and expensive; points-trading is rational and profitable
mechanism: Focusing on target-price reduces overtrading; allows time for confluent signals to develop
assumptions: Patience and selectivity outperform frequent trading
failure_modes: Waiting for high-probability setups may miss fast-moving trends
